notes.b: Bones only help the body move where they meet other bones. These meeting places are called joints, and they are grouped by how much movement they allow.
points: A joint is a place where two or more bones meet. Joints are grouped by how much movement they allow, from none at all to a wide range.

Fixed (immovable) joints join bones with fibrous tissue and allow no movement, so they protect and hold structures rigid, for example the sutures of the cranium (the joins between the bones of the skull).

Slightly movable (cartilaginous) joints join bones with cartilage (a firm, flexible tissue) and allow a little movement, for example between vertebrae, which are joined by intervertebral discs. There is more on this in The axial skeleton.
Freely movable (synovial) joints have bones separated by a fluid-filled cavity and allow a wide range of movement, for example the shoulder, elbow, hip and knee.
notes.tip: You may be asked to name a fixed joint and a slightly movable joint: use the sutures of the cranium and the joints between vertebrae.

notes.b: Not all freely movable joints move in the same way. Their types are named after the shape of the surfaces and the movement this allows.
points: Ball-and-socket joints (shoulder, hip): a rounded head fits into a cup, so movement is possible in all directions and the limb can also rotate.
Hinge joints (elbow, knee): movement is in one plane only, bending and straightening, like a door opening and closing on its hinge.

Pivot joints: one bone rotates around another, for example the atlas (the top vertebra) turning on the axis (the second vertebra) to turn the head, and the radius turning against the ulna to rotate the forearm.
Gliding joints: flat surfaces slide over each other, for example between the small wrist and ankle bones, so only small sliding movements are possible.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to name a ball-and-socket joint and a hinge joint and say where each is found: shoulder or hip, and elbow or knee.

notes.h: Structure and function of a synovial joint: cartilage, membrane and fluid
notes.b: A synovial joint has to move smoothly thousands of times without the bone ends wearing away. Three parts working together make this possible: the cartilage on the bone ends, the membrane that makes the fluid, and the fluid itself.
points: Articular cartilage (hyaline cartilage) is a smooth, slippery, slightly compressible layer covering the ends of the bones inside the joint.
Articular cartilage reduces friction so the bones glide over each other, absorbs shock to cushion the bones against impact, and prevents the bone ends from wearing each other away.
Cartilage has no blood vessels, so it gets its nutrients from the synovial fluid and heals slowly if it is damaged.
The synovial membrane is a thin membrane lining the inside of the joint capsule, but it does not cover the cartilage. It secretes synovial fluid into the joint cavity.
Synovial fluid is a thick, slippery fluid filling the joint cavity. It lubricates the joint, reducing friction and wear, and helps absorb shock.
Synovial fluid also supplies oxygen and nutrients to the cartilage and removes its wastes, which is how cartilage stays alive without a blood supply of its own.
notes.tip: The membrane makes the fluid; the cartilage does not. Don't say the synovial membrane covers the cartilage. When asked for the function of synovial fluid, give lubrication and also nourishing the cartilage.

notes.h: Structure and function of a synovial joint: capsule, ligaments, tendons and menisci
notes.b: Smooth surfaces are not enough: the joint must also be held together and be moved by muscles. The capsule and ligaments hold the bones in place, tendons connect the muscles that move them, and in the knee fibrocartilage pads add extra cushioning.
points: The joint capsule is a tough, fibrous sleeve that encloses the joint, holds the synovial fluid in and helps hold the bones together. It is strengthened by ligaments.
Ligaments are tough, strong bands of fibrous connective tissue, mainly collagen with some elastic fibres, that join bone to bone across the joint.

Ligaments hold the bones of the joint together and keep them in line. Being slightly elastic, they allow the joint to move in its normal directions while limiting movement in others, which prevents dislocation (the bones being forced out of position).
Some ligaments lie outside the capsule and some inside the joint, for example inside the knee.

Tendons are tough, strong, inelastic (non-stretchy) cords of fibrous connective tissue, mainly collagen, that join muscle to bone. The Achilles tendon, for example, joins the calf muscle to the heel bone.
A tendon transmits the pull of a contracting muscle to the bone, so the bone moves at the joint. Because it does not stretch, all of the muscle's pull goes into moving the bone.
Pads of fibrocartilage (cartilage with extra tough fibres) inside some joints, the menisci in the knee, deepen the joint surfaces, spread the load and absorb shock.

Diagram: a generalised synovial joint (or the knee or hip) in section, labelling the two bones, articular cartilage, joint cavity with synovial fluid, synovial membrane, joint capsule, ligament, and a tendon attaching a muscle to one bone.
notes.tip: A ligament joins bone to bone and a tendon joins muscle to bone; students often reverse them. Ligaments are slightly elastic but tendons are inelastic, so never call a tendon elastic.

notes.h: How the parts of a joint work together: the knee
notes.b: The knee shows how every part of a synovial joint has its own job and how they combine to let the leg move without the joint falling apart.
points: At the knee, articular cartilage on the femur (thigh bone), tibia (shin bone) and the back of the patella (kneecap), together with the synovial fluid, lets the bones glide over each other.
Ligaments inside and outside the joint keep the femur and tibia aligned and stop the knee bending sideways or backwards.
The quadriceps tendon, which contains the patella, passes the pull of the thigh muscle to the tibia to straighten the leg.

notes.b: Ligaments, tendons and cartilage are all tough tissues found at joints, so they are easily confused. They differ in what they join, how much they stretch and the job they do.
points: What each joins: a ligament joins bone to bone; a tendon joins muscle to bone; cartilage either covers the ends of bones (articular cartilage) or joins bones (discs).
Elasticity: a ligament is slightly elastic, allowing some movement; a tendon is inelastic, so it transmits force without wasting it; cartilage is firm but compressible, so it absorbs shock.
Main function: a ligament holds the joint together and prevents dislocation; a tendon moves the bone when the muscle contracts; cartilage reduces friction and absorbs shock.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to distinguish between a ligament and a tendon. Give what each joins and whether it is elastic, as a paired comparison.

notes.h: Antagonistic muscle pairs: why and how
notes.b: Muscles can only do one thing: shorten. That limitation is why the body arranges muscles in opposing pairs around each joint.
points: A muscle can only contract and pull, never push, so each movement at a joint needs a second muscle to pull the bone back.
An antagonistic pair is two muscles that produce opposite movements at the same joint: when one contracts, the other relaxes and is stretched.
The flexor bends a joint (flexion); the extensor straightens it (extension).
Each muscle is attached by tendons at both ends. The origin is the attachment to the bone that stays still; the insertion is the attachment to the bone that moves.
When the muscle contracts it shortens (and becomes fatter), pulling the insertion towards the origin and so moving the bone.
notes.tip: A relaxed muscle does not push or lengthen itself: it is stretched by the contraction of its antagonist. To explain why muscles work in pairs, say that a muscle can only pull.

notes.h: Antagonistic pairs in action: the elbow and the knee
notes.b: The biceps and triceps in the upper arm are the standard example of an antagonistic pair, and the thigh muscles at the knee are a second one.
points: At the elbow, the biceps lies at the front of the upper arm, with its origin on the scapula (shoulder blade) and its insertion on the radius.
The triceps lies at the back of the upper arm, with its origin on the scapula and humerus and its insertion on the ulna.
Bending the arm (flexion): the biceps contracts and shortens, pulling the radius and forearm up, while the triceps relaxes and is stretched. The biceps is the flexor.
Straightening the arm (extension): the triceps contracts, pulling the ulna and forearm down, while the biceps relaxes and is stretched. The triceps is the extensor.
A second example is the knee: the quadriceps (front of the thigh) contracts to straighten the leg, as the extensor, and the hamstrings (back of the thigh) contract to bend it, as the flexor.
notes.tip: In flexion of the elbow the biceps contracts and the triceps relaxes: never say both contract or that the triceps pushes. The biceps inserts on the radius and the triceps on the ulna, not both on the humerus.

notes.h: Lever action, coordination and drawing the arm
notes.b: The arm works as a lever, and the nervous system controls the pair so that movement is smooth or the joint is held still.
points: Lever action: the forearm acts as a lever with the elbow joint as the pivot (the fixed point it turns around).
The biceps is inserted close to the elbow, so a small shortening of the muscle moves the hand through a large distance quickly, at the cost of needing a large muscle force.
Coordination: the nervous system sends impulses to one muscle of the pair while the other is allowed to relax, so movements are smooth.
Both muscles of a pair contracting slightly together hold a joint steady in one position, for example when holding a weight still.

Diagram: two drawings of the arm, bent and straight, showing scapula, humerus, radius, ulna, elbow joint, biceps and triceps with their tendons, each muscle labelled contracted or relaxed in each position, with arrows showing the direction of pull.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to explain what an antagonistic pair is, with a named example, and to describe how it bends and straightens a limb. Name both muscles and say which contracts and which relaxes each time.

notes.h: Modelling an antagonistic pair: building and using it
notes.b: A simple model of the arm lets you see antagonistic muscles work. Each part of the model stands for a real part of the arm.
points: A simple physical model uses two strips of stiff card or wood to represent the upper arm (humerus) and the forearm (radius and ulna), joined at one end by a split pin, which represents the elbow hinge joint.

Two pieces of string, elastic bands or long balloons represent the biceps and triceps. Each is fixed to the upper arm at one end (origin) and to the forearm at the other (insertion), one on the front and one on the back, with their ends standing for tendons.
Pulling (shortening) the front string raises the forearm while the back string slackens. This shows the biceps contracting and the triceps relaxing in flexion.
Pulling the back string lowers the forearm, showing extension.
Pushing on a string does nothing, which shows that a muscle can only pull.

The model shows that muscles work in pairs with opposite effects, that a muscle must be attached on both sides of a joint to move it, and that an insertion close to the joint gives a large movement of the forearm end (the lever action).
notes.tip: Modelling an antagonistic pair is new to this specification, so be ready to say what each part of the model represents and what the model shows.

notes.h: Evaluating the model of an antagonistic pair
notes.b: No model is perfect. Judging a model means saying what it leaves out or gets wrong compared with the real arm.
points: Real muscles shorten actively by contracting and get fatter, while the model's strings are pulled by hand.
The model has no articular cartilage, synovial fluid or ligaments, so it does not show how the joint surfaces glide or how the bones are held together.
A split pin allows movement in only one plane and does not show the rotation of the radius.
The model has no nervous control and no energy supply (ATP), whereas real muscles need impulses to contract and ATP as their energy source.
Real tendons are inelastic, while elastic bands stretch.
notes.tip: When asked to evaluate the model, give limitations as pairs: what the real arm does and how the model differs.

keyTerms.definition: A freely movable joint in which the bones are separated by a fluid-filled joint cavity.
The smooth, slippery layer of cartilage covering the bone ends inside a synovial joint.
The thick, slippery fluid in the joint cavity that lubricates the joint and nourishes the cartilage.
The thin membrane lining the joint capsule that secretes synovial fluid.
The tough, fibrous sleeve that encloses a synovial joint and holds the synovial fluid in.
A tough, slightly elastic band of fibrous tissue that joins bone to bone.
A tough, inelastic cord of fibrous tissue that joins muscle to bone and transmits the muscle's pull.
Two muscles that produce opposite movements at the same joint, so that one contracts while the other relaxes.
A muscle that bends a joint.
A muscle that straightens a joint.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a ligament and a tendon in terms of what each joins, its elasticity and its function.
questions.model: A ligament joins bone to bone, whereas a tendon joins muscle to bone. A ligament is slightly elastic, allowing some movement, whereas a tendon is inelastic, so it transmits the full pull of the contracting muscle. A ligament holds the bones of a joint together and prevents dislocation; a tendon moves the bone when the muscle contracts.

questions.prompt: Draw a labelled diagram of a synovial joint and relate the functions of cartilage, ligaments, synovial fluid and tendons to the working of the joint.
questions.model: The diagram should show the two bones, articular cartilage on the bone ends, the joint cavity containing synovial fluid, the synovial membrane lining the joint capsule, the joint capsule, a ligament joining the two bones, and a tendon joining a muscle to one bone. Articular cartilage is smooth and slippery, reducing friction so the bones glide, and it absorbs shock. Synovial fluid lubricates the joint, reducing friction and wear, and supplies nutrients to the cartilage. Ligaments hold the bones together and keep them in line, allowing movement in the normal directions while preventing dislocation. Tendons transmit the pull of the muscle to the bone, so the bone moves at the joint without any loss of force, because they do not stretch.

questions.prompt: Describe a model you could use to show how an antagonistic muscle pair works at the elbow. Explain what it shows and give two limitations.
questions.model: Two strips of stiff card represent the upper arm and forearm, joined at one end by a split pin as the elbow hinge. Two strings are fixed to the upper arm at one end and to the forearm at the other, one on the front to represent the biceps and one on the back to represent the triceps. Pulling the front string shortens it, raising the forearm, which shows flexion with the biceps contracting and the triceps relaxing. Pulling the back string lowers the forearm, showing extension with the triceps contracting and the biceps relaxing. The model shows that muscles work in pairs with opposite effects and that a muscle can only pull. Two limitations: the model has no articular cartilage, synovial fluid or ligaments; and a split pin allows movement in only one plane and does not show the rotation of the radius.
